  holding the best gun: a good shot's +1.9 against a rarely fighting doctor's -0.6 is worth 1.72, suggested; +1.0 against
  -1.0 between two who fight alike is worth nothing, not suggested (tested, with random colonies: nobody left without a
  weapon who had one, no weapon to two, trades in pairs). A trade is weighed against what storage gave its two: worth more,
  it replaces that, and storage is shared again among the rest. The line says both sides: "Charge rifle to Ana (+1.9),
  Bautista takes her revolver (-0.6): the colony gains, and Bautista rarely fights."; the one who gives up some has no
  reasons of their own, the colony's are theirs.
- **A lucky weapon or an heirloom, never a bar** (`PickColonist.Keepsakes`): Rimfolk's lucky-item quirk on a weapon
  (`Quirks/LuckyItems.cs`; its mood comes with any weapon of its kind on them, so another of the kind keeps it, and with
  Simple Sidearms the weapon set down is kept as a sidearm when it fits its weights) and an heirloom carried
  (`Lives/Legacy.cs`, the heir's comfort or anyone's), read only while those moods are on. Giving one up costs a little in
  the choice (0.04 of a point for each point of mood between having it and not, at most 0.4: a lucky weapon's +3 and -4 is
  0.28), where it weighs one weapon or trade against another (another autopistol keeping the luck may win over a slightly
  better rifle), never against the threshold or a trade's rules, so it never stops a suggestion on its own; the line
  always says it, with the real numbers:
  "Bautista would be upset to give up his lucky autopistol (mood -4 without it, +3 with it)". Persona bonds stay as before.
- **Trades proposed by the colonists** (`WeaponAsks.cs`, "Colonists ask for better weapons", pool
  `Rimfolk_Pool_WeaponTrade`): when a colonist has no stored weapon to ask for, their best trade that stands where one of
  the two gains 1.2 or more, the asks' own waits and chance; then said to the other once the two are together
  (`Together.When`, up to four hours), both safe and both weapons still in their hands as the words say. The one who gains
  asks ("Bautista, that charge rifle would do more in my hands, will you take my revolver?"), the one who gives up some offers
  ("You should have this charge rifle, Ana, I can barely aim it.", tagged for a low skill or rarely fighting only when so),
  two who both gain propose it; every age, every tone, one sentence each. Nobody asks for a suggestion that gives up their
  own lucky weapon or heirloom; the other may still propose the trade, its line warning of it. The inbox's quiet row: "Ana
  proposed a trade to Bautista: her revolver for his charge rifle (+1.9)", its act the trade's order; the gear tab's row is
  tagged "Asked for". A trade proposed is kept as the colonist's last ask (with the other's id, `WeaponAskNote.other`).
- **Tests**: `Tools/Tests/WeaponShowTests.cs` (the qualities' colours, the card's tile, Nice Inventory Tab's widths at every
  tab width it allows, the room the box makes, where the row goes, the seams); `WeaponPickTests.cs` (how much each fights,
  trades for the colony, a lucky weapon and an heirloom, the trades' pool in every age).

### A full kit for every colonist (the player's request, 9 November 2026)

The player, with a picture of Avila's gear in Nice Inventory Tab (an autopistol and a belt, no melee weapon, and the quiet
line "No better weapon in storage"): "the mod should also recognize if a pawn has no melee/ranged sidearm equipped and then
offer one from the inventory. the pawns should always have a ranged and melee weapon, assuming they have no restrictions,
and suggest/equip them accordingly. also offhand if they have capacity & compatibility". Released 0.189.0.

- **The kit** (`Weapons/WeaponKitMath.cs`, pure, tested in `Tools/Tests/WeaponKitTests.cs`): with Simple Sidearms every
  colonist who can fight carries one ranged and one melee weapon, one in hand and the other as a sidearm; with Dual Wield, a
  weapon in the off hand where their hands, the weapons and the mod's rules allow it and it adds something. Without Simple
  Sidearms the kit is the one weapon in hand (a vanilla colonist holds one), without Dual Wield there is no off hand. Each
  slot is filled (the weapon in hand of its kind, or a sidearm Simple Sidearms remembers; a one-use launcher never counts),
  missing, or not for them and why (`KitView`, `KitBar`).
- **Restrictions decide the kit, and it never fights them:** incapable of violence, no kit; incapable of shooting or a
  brawler, melee only; a kind their Ideology role bars (the game's `RoleEffect_NoRangedWeapons` and `NoMeleeWeapons`,
  `PickColonist.RoleNoRanged` and `RoleNoMelee`, now also in `WeaponPickMath.Score`), none of it; a weapon the game refuses
  them (`EquipmentUtility.CanEquip`: coded, bonded, a race's rule as Humanoid Alien Races adds it, a role's), one their
  faith despises, a heavy weapon they can't carry, never (each `PickOption.Cant`); a sidearm only within Simple Sidearms'
  weights (its default preset: 2.7 kg a gun, 1.9 kg a blade), never a one-use launcher or one on an outfit stand (its job
  takes it from the ground), and never one its own `CanPickupSidearmInstance` refuses them now (asked of each stored weapon
  light enough, `PickOption.SidearmCant`: its weight modes, slots and their free room as set); an off-hand weapon only where
  Dual Wield's `CanBeOffHand` allows it, not `IsTwoHand`, of the main hand's kind (both hands fire or swing together), never
  beside a two-handed main weapon and never with a hand or arm missing (its own `HasMissingArmOrHand` rule, read from the
  game's missing parts).
- **A missing kind is a gap, filled even under the usual threshold** (0.6), but never with something nearly useless: the
  least is 2.0 for them (`Floor`, twice bare hands, `WeaponPickMath.Unarmed`; their own score with skill, traits, passion
  and the fights you meet; "poor" on the rating's scale runs up to 3.5), a shooter's blade must beat their gun's own blows
  (its "in melee" rating, a rifle's butt about 3.0) by 0.3 (`OverBash`), and an off-hand weapon must add 0.3 to both hands
  together over the main hand alone (`OffHandAdds`, Dual Wield's penalties in). The weapon chosen is the best for the part
  it plays (`RoleScore`, never the minimum): in hand, their own score; a sidearm half its "sidearm" situation over its
  overall (light and handy), a quick blade a fifth of a point more (a shooter's melee sidearm), a gun a tenth of its
  "kiting" situation over its overall (a melee fighter's gun to finish or kite with). With nothing in hand and both kinds
  missing, the kind they would rather hold (a gun when they shoot at least as well as they fight hand to hand) goes in
  hand, the other as a sidearm.
- **Where it comes from:** storage (as before; forbidden weapons are read too, never suggested or taken, only asked for and
  named where nothing fills a slot, `ForbiddenFills`); their own pack (a weapon Simple Sidearms doesn't remember, which its
  own unloading would carry to storage, `WeaponMods.Unremembered`, read as its `FirstUnloadableThing` reads its memory:
  kept as a sidearm, no walk, `PickKind.Keep`, a third of a point in its favour when choosing); another colonist's spare
  (`Spares`: a weapon they carry beyond their own kit, each kind they don't hold keeping its best; never a lucky weapon, an
  heirloom, a bonded weapon or a one-use launcher, none from someone set aside; `PickKind.Spare`, a third of a point against
  it when choosing, so storage comes first).
- **The colony's choice fills the kit first** (`WeaponPickMath.Assign`): those with nothing in hand are served first in the
  greedy, take any weapon sensible for them, and no exchange leaves them unarmed (a move that arms one always wins, taking if
  need be a weapon given as another's upgrade; tested against brute force with the kit first, then the most gain); the
  weapons the other empty slots would take are kept from everyone's upgrades (`Reserve`), those whose off hand is to be
  filled keep their main hand this round, those whose sidearm's kind follows their main hand trade only for the same kind.
  Then the empty slots are filled for real, each one's worth by how much they fight (`FightWeight`), so the front line is
  served first when weapons are short; then upgrades and trades as before, then a sidearm they carry bettered. A trade may
  arm someone holding a weapon they mustn't use.
- **Shown:** the gear tab's row (`WeaponPickGearTab.Row`) gets the missing case: tagged **Missing**, its headline what is
  missing and how it is filled ("No melee weapon: steel hatchet as a sidearm"; the rating is the badge beside it, the
  Defenses page's head says "(3.8)"), the same picture, rating and reasons ("she has nothing for close work, and it's
  light enough to carry beside her autopistol"), the right button (Equip, As sidearm, Off hand, **Keep as sidearm**, **Take
  from** whom). The quiet line is honest about the kit: an empty slot nothing fills is said, "No melee weapon in storage for
  Avila" (both kinds: "No weapon in storage"), under the rows too (Nice Inventory Tab's row height follows,
  `WeaponNiceMath.Height`'s `gapLine`), its tooltip what was looked at and why each was left out (`Looked`, `KitLeftOut`:
  forbidden, the game's refusal, past the sidearm's weight, Simple Sidearms' refusal, one-use, on an outfit stand, too weak
  for them, no better than the gun's butt, adds too little in the off hand, not allowed there, two-handed, going to someone
  else); "No better weapon in storage" when the kit is full. The Defenses page: each colonist's kit at a glance under their
  name (`WeaponKitWords.Chips`: ranged, melee and with Dual Wield the off hand, each its picture and rating for them,
  missing, or a dash with why on the tooltip), how many kits are full, and **Fill every kit (n)**, which only gives the
  orders (`WeaponPick.DoKit`). The weapon card's "Who should carry this": who lacks its kind first ("she has no melee
  weapon (+3.0)").
- **Colonists fill a gap themselves** (`Weapons/WeaponKitSelf.cs`, "Colonists fill an empty weapon slot themselves",
  `weaponKitSelf`, on): at their hourly look on the suggestions' own slice (`Sched.RareWeaponPicks`, no new slot), in their
  free time at home and safe (`WeaponAsks.FreeAndSafe`: not drafted, downed, asleep or in a mental state, no threat on the
  map or near), at most once a day each (`WeaponPickBook.fetched`, saved, pruned daily), a colonist with an empty slot the
  choice fills from storage starts a real job of their own accord (`StartJob`, not an order): the game's `Equip` into an
  empty hand only, Simple Sidearms' `EquipSecondary`, Dual Wield's `DW_EquipOffhand`; a weapon already in their pack is
  remembered at once. Never in place of a weapon they hold, never forbidden, never what something stops now
  (`WeaponPick.WhyNot`: a path, burning, reserved, Simple Sidearms' refusal), never a persona weapon that would bond, never
  one their faith despises (out of the choice). The game's apparel policy covers apparel only, so it has no say over
  weapons. A line as they pick it up (the job's finish action, on success; `Rimfolk_Pool_WeaponKitTake`, tagged hand,
  sidearm, offhand or keep and the kind, every age and tone). Off, an empty slot is only suggested.
- **Colonists who ask** gain a reason, "kit" (`Rimfolk_Pool_WeaponAsk`, every age, ranged, melee and the off hand: "I've
  nothing for close work, can I take the knife in the stockpile?"), under the same waits and chance, whatever the gain;
  only when they don't fill it themselves (the setting off, or something they can't take on their own: a forbidden weapon,
  one on an outfit stand for a sidearm, one in place of what they hold, a persona weapon). A forbidden weapon asked for has
  a quiet row in This week whose act allows it.
- **Simple Sidearms by name** (`WeaponMods`): its memory read (`rememberedWeapons`, each pair once, the one in hand first),
  told of a sidearm kept (`GetMemoryCompForPawn`, `InformOfAddedSidearm`), its refusal asked (`CanPickupSidearmInstance`).
  A spare handed over (`Rimfolk_TakeSpareWeapon`, `JobDriver_TakeSpareWeapon` in `Weapons/WeaponSwapJob.cs`): the one
  taking it walks to the one who carries it, who hands it over from their pack, into an empty hand or else the pack; both
  memories told by name.
- **Saved:** `WeaponPickBook.fetched` (colonist: tick, a day), modelled in `Tools/save_estimate.py`. No new Harmony patch,
  no new Sched slot.

## Armour and apparel you can judge at a glance (the player's request, 9 November 2026)

"And maybe after you can do the whole thing, the same thing for armor and apparel." The plan is `docs/design/apparel.md`.
Step 1 (0.187.0) built the rating (`Apparel/ApparelRateMath.cs`), the tags (`ApparelTagMath.cs`) and the review of every
piece in the player's mods (`docs/apparel/`). Step 2 (point 5) brings it into the game, after the player's screenshot of
the game's plain card for a "Bluefur parka (awful)": "i don't see the gear cards in game by default, is this implemented
at all?" Step 3 (point 6, recommendations) is built, below ("Step 3: better armour and clothes for each colonist").

- **One reading for the review and the game.** What a piece's defs say is plain data (`Apparel/ApparelReadMath.cs`, pure):
  `ApparelDefFacts` (its stat bases and equipped offsets, stuff categories, layers, groups and tags, its apparel
  properties, its comps and mod extensions as class names with simple fields, lists of names and maps of stats, its verbs
  and their projectiles, the abilities it grants, the titles' and faiths' apparel rules it meets, whether it is made or
  worn by a faction, the patches the review doesn't apply, its stuff and the stuffs it is also rated in, and for the
  piece in hand its quality's factors, hit points, a dead wearer, the moods those give and whom it is biocoded to).
  `ApparelRead.Facts` turns them into the rating's own facts (the review's `Inputs.Facts`, moved here: comps through
  `ApparelRateMath.ReadComp`, verbs through `PowerOfVerb`, hediffs' stages, VEF's apparel extension, the code-only comps
  named and marked rough); `ApparelRead.Full` rates it in its usual stuff with its role judged in plain stuff, rates it in
  its other stuffs, and gives its tags, line and table. `Tools/ApparelReview/Inputs.cs` is now only the JSON to facts, and
  `Program.cs` rates through `ApparelRead.Full`; regenerating gives `docs/apparel/apparel.json` and `README.md` byte for
  byte (checked), so the game's rules are the review's for all 509 rated pieces. The usual stuff (devilstrand for
  fabric, steel, plain leather, wood, granite) and the common stuffs of each kind are the extractor's own lists, ported.
- **The live def as facts** (`Apparel/ApparelLive.cs`): its stat bases, offsets, comps (the piece in hand's own comps'
  numbers over its props', so A RimWorld of Magic's rolled enchantment counts), extensions, verbs (a projectile's damage
  and piercing by its own `GetDamageAmount` and `GetArmorPenetration`), abilities (the game's apparel abilities and a
  comp's lists), the apparel rules of royal titles, memes and roles (read once by field name as the extractor reads them),
  recipes and pawn kinds; its equipped offsets as the game gives them (`StatWorker.StatOffsetFromGear` for a thing, the
  stat's parts for a kind); its quality's factors on armour and insulation by the game's own stats for this piece or kind,
  stuff and quality (`StatRequest.For`), as the game's value over the rating's own sum of base and stuff, from a stat
  not held at its 200% cap. Types' names as defs write them (a plain `CompProperties` by its comp class). Kept by def,
  stuff and quality; by the piece itself only where it differs from its kind (worn below half its hit points, taken from
  the dead, enchanted, biocoded), an hour of the game's time or until its wear stage changes. All forgotten with a new game.
- **The piece in hand** (`ApparelRead.Facts`, the rating's `Moods`): the game's `ThoughtWorker_ApparelDamaged` thresholds
  (below half its hit points, below a fifth; only where its wearer cares, `careIfDamaged`) and `ThoughtWorker_DeadMansApparel`
  give their moods from the game's own thought stages; a mood point counts as the mental break threshold moved by a
  hundredth (`ApparelRateMath.WorthPerMood`, 0.015), in the mind, and is named among the effects. Wear doesn't weaken armour
  in the game (`ArmorUtility.ApplyArmor`: every hit that reaches a piece wears it by a quarter of its damage, its armour is
  its stat), so the card says so rather than lowering the rating for it. Biocoding names whom it is coded to.
- **For a colonist** (`Apparel/ApparelForMath.cs`, pure; the wearer read by `ApparelLive.Wearer`): steps from the usual
  rating that add up. How they fight (a gun in hand a shooter, a blade a melee fighter; else a brawler in melee, and their
  skills four levels apart; incapable of violence only lasting and walking; can't shoot, melee): the fight as the rating
  works it out for that wearer, so a shield belt is 1.0 for a shooter. Their body: zones whose groups no part of theirs
  carries any more are left out of where hits land (`ApparelForMath.BodyWithout`). Their weather (`ApparelLive.Climate`:
  outside now; the season's three twelfths at the tile, `GenTemperature.AverageTemperatureAtTileForTwelfth`, less and more
  the sun's 7 °C swing): warmth and cooling count by what the season asks of this piece beyond what they keep wearing (their
  `ComfyTemperatureMin` and `Max` now, the insulation and comfort offsets of what it would replace and of itself taken back
  out): the degrees asked with the role's weight and one more (the review's "in the cold"), the degrees beyond at a fifth of
  the role's weight (`ApparelForMath.ClimateWorth`). Moods it would add: the apparel-damaged mood is one, at the worst stage
  of what they wear, so a worn piece adds nothing to someone whose other clothes are as worn; the other gender's
  (`WrongApparelGender`) unless something else they keep already gives it. What it would take the place of: what they wear
  that `ApparelUtility.CanWearTogether` says can't stay, each rated for them. What stops them: `EquipmentUtility.CanEquip`
  for a piece in hand (biocoded to another, their role, their age), the developmental stage and
  `ApparelUtility.HasPartsToWear` for a kind. Kept an hour.
- **The info card** (`ApparelInfoCard.cs`): a pass-through postfix on `ThingDef.SpecialDisplayStats` in its own
  `StatCategoryDef` (`Rimfolk_ApparelRating`, display order 0): the rating (band, rough or not, whom it is rated for), a
  shooter's and a melee fighter's where they differ by half a point, each sub-rating, the line, each tag with why and its
  rule, the effects, the piece's hit points left with the game's thresholds and days of wear, and the wearer's or
  carrier's own rating with its steps. A postfix on `Dialog_InfoCard.DoWindowContents` draws "Rimfolk's apparel card" at
  the foot.
- **Rimfolk's apparel card** (`ApparelCardWindow.cs`, key "ApparelCard", least 440 by 460, on `UI/ItemCardWindow.cs`):
  the item card's base keeps the thing, kind, stuff and colonist (the last chosen remembered), the scroll and the error
  handling, and draws what item cards share: the head (`UiKit.ItemPortrait` large in its quality's frame, the badge, band
  and role, how it is rated, "All the game's stats", a second quiet line, the line in plain words), meters, situation bars,
  effects, rows of numbers, the colonist's heading and picking. The weapon card can move onto it unchanged in what it
  shows, and an item card for everything after it. The apparel card adds: the tags as chips; the sub-ratings; protection by
  body part (three armour meters held at 200%; `ApparelUi.DrawFigure`, a figure of eight regions from
  `ApparelForMath.Regions` filled by how much of each it covers, beside each region's share of the shots and its cover);
  warmth against the weather (its warmth and cooling, outside now and the season's range, the comfortable range with it on
  for the colonist or worn alone over a bare human, a strip with the season shaded, the comfort framed and now marked, a
  verdict); the piece as it is (quality, material, hit points with a bar marked at the game's two thresholds and their
  stage labels and moods, days of wear, wear and armour, from the dead, biocoded); other materials (`ByStuff`, its own
  marked); situations; effects; key numbers; and the colonist (rating, steps, how they fight and why, their body, the other
  gender, and what it would take the place of, a click opening that piece's card). Worked out for a colonist once every two
  seconds.
- **Open it first** (`ApparelCardFirst.cs`): the weapons' one prefix on `WindowStack.Add` (`Patch_WeaponCardFirst`) now
  asks the weapon card and then the apparel card; a def is one or the other. Its own let-through for "All the game's
  stats"; navigation inside the game's card stays the game's (`WeaponCardFirst.insideGameCard`, shared). Setting
  `apparelCardFirst`.
- **The gear tab** (`ApparelGearTab.cs`, "Ratings on the gear tab"): the game's `ITab_Pawn_Gear.DrawThingRow` gives up 56
  pixels at an apparel row's end for the badge and the card's button (a patch class of its own beside the weapons');
  Nice Inventory Tab (decompiled from the player's upload, read by name, never run): its `EquippedItem` rows (the legacy
  layout's apparel box, belts and shields in its equipment box) get the badge on the picture and the button at its corner
  as weapons do, its `InventoryItem` cells (apparel carried) the same; its `ApparelGridSlot` (the alternative layout's apparel
  grid, whose `Draw` opens the game's card on a left click, puts its warning mark at the top left, its stars at the top's
  middle, its lock and drop buttons at the right corners and its wear bar at the foot) gets the badge alone at its top left,
  under the warning mark when its private `problems` shows one; the badge's click is caught in a prefix and opens
  Rimfolk's card. Each Nice Inventory Tab patch returns no target without the mod and stands down on purpose.
- **Settings** (How you're told, Apparel; each on): `apparelRatings` "Apparel ratings" (the master; needs the deeper game
  hooks), `apparelGearTab` "Ratings on the gear tab", `apparelCardFirst` "Open Rimfolk's apparel card first". No saved
  game data, no Sched slot.
- **Text:** `Languages/English/Keyed/Rimfolk_Apparel.xml` (the words the weapon card shares are its keys); the tags' labels
  and reasons and the line stay English from the math, as the weapons'. The Almanac's "judging armour and clothes"
  (Defending).
- **Tests:** `Tools/Tests/ApparelLiveTests.cs` (681 checks): thirteen of the base game's pieces (flak vest, shield belt,
  jump pack, smokepop pack, parka, duster, tuque, cowboy hat, psychic foil helmet, marine armor, recon helmet, tribalwear,
  T-shirt) built as the live reader builds them rate as `apparel.json` has them in every field (rating, a shooter's and a
  melee fighter's, role, whom for, slot, table, every sub-rating and situation, tags and their reasons, the line, the
  specials, the rating by stuff, armour, insulation, coverage, rough or not, the usual stuff); the extractor's stuff lists;
  quality, the 200% cap, wear and its moods, a dead wearer, biocoding; a colonist's rating by how they fight, their body,
  their weather, the moods it adds, and its steps adding up; regions; and the seams (settings, keys made from words, hooks,
  frame, Almanac).

### Step 3: better armour and clothes for each colonist, and colonists who ask (point 6)

The plan the player approved (9 November 2026): "Better armour and clothes for each colonist from what the colony has, by
their role, the season and the raids met, their faith's and title's apparel rules, their body; one click to wear it;
colonists sometimes ask, rarely." From their game: "Need warm clothes" and "Tattered apparel" showing at -25 °C in winter,
Bautista in a ratty shirt. Built as the weapons' step 3 was (above), on the colonist's own rating of step 2. Released 0.196.0.

- **The choice, pure** (`Apparel/ApparelPickMath.cs`, tested in `Tools/Tests/ApparelPickTests.cs`). A colonist with a piece
  is scored by their own rating (`ApparelForMath.For`: how they fight, their body, their weather, the moods it adds) plus
  what the colony's life asks of it: a rule of theirs not met now that it meets (their title's or role's apparel they
  lack, 1.5; their faith's desired apparel, 0.6), their work (clothes that speed it by 3% or more, 0.4; slow it, -0.3, by
  `WorkLean`: their general work speed and their work's own stats, a doctor's tending and surgery, a cook's cooking and
  food poisoning, a grower's, miner's, builder's, researcher's, crafter's, a warden's and talker's social stats), and for
  armour (body armour, helmets, off-hand shields) the raids met: its mechanoids' and melee situations over its overall by
  the shares of mechanoid raids and of crowds of people or tribes (half and two fifths), at most a point either way, by
  how much they fight. A piece's gain is over what it would take the place of (the game's `CanWearTogether`), judged in
  each replaced piece's own role (`ApparelForMath.For` gained a role to judge it as: marine armour in place of a flak vest
  and a parka gains as armour and loses as a coat; the same steps on that role's weights and scale), or over nothing (1.0).
  Never a choice: what they can't wear, what would take off a piece they locked or one they wear for a rule it doesn't
  meet too, what leaves them colder or hotter than they can bear over the season ahead (`KeepsComfort`), what their outfit
  doesn't allow (said apart, below).
- **The season ahead** (`ApparelPick.Ahead`, `ApparelPickMath.Margin`): outside now and the coldest night and hottest day of
  this twelfth and the next two (`AverageTemperatureAtTileForTwelfth` less and more the sun's 7 °C), as the game's own
  `Alert_NeedWarmClothes` looks three twelfths ahead. Against their least and most comfortable temperatures in what they
  wear now, counted only where the cold goes under 5 °C (the game's alert's own line) or the heat over 30 °C: degrees short,
  and degrees to spare. The rating's own "their weather" (the card's) is unchanged.
- **Gaps first** (`Gaps`, `Fills`), each filled with anything rated 2.0 or more for them: warmth for anyone 1 °C or more short
  (a piece adding 3 °C or all that is lacking, net of what it replaces), the most lacking first, the warmest first, a coat
  then a hat (two pieces a round); cooling the same; in a raid-heavy colony (`RaidHeavyAt`: the raids weighed by recency
  as the weapons weigh them, two this month or four in sixty days), body armour and a helmet for those who fight more than
  rarely (`Fights` above 0.5) and wear none, the most fighting first; each worn piece below half its hit points or taken
  from the dead, replaced by any piece not itself as worn and no worse once its wear's mood is counted.
- **Then upgrades**: 0.8 of a point or more in place of what it replaces (`Threshold`; a little more than the weapons' 0.6,
  as changing clothes leaves the old piece behind and the season moves a rating by a few tenths: a flak helmet over a
  simple one is suggested, marine armour over recon, or a good parka over a normal one, are not); a piece for an empty slot
  that is no gap only when it rates 6.0 or more for them on its own (`AddOnAt`) or meets a rule of theirs not met now (the
  game's own apparel optimizer fills empty slots with what an outfit allows). Greedily by gain, armour's weighed by how much
  each fights (at least a fifth). Alike pieces (one report: kind, stuff, quality, wear; one place) weighed once.
- **One assignment for the colony** (`Assign`): no piece to two colonists; a colonist's pieces fit together (`Fits`, the game's
  rule: no shared layer over a shared body part group) and never take the place of the same worn piece. Then trades of
  armour between two (body armour for body armour, a helmet for a helmet), as the weapons trade: better for both (0.3
  each, 0.8 together), or one gains a point and the colony 0.8 weighed by how much each fights (a doctor in recon armour
  who rarely fights, a front-line fighter in a flak vest); each takes only the other's in place of their own, both
  allowed by their outfits, neither locked or kept for a rule. Tested on 300 random colonies: no piece to two, nothing they
  can't wear or their outfit doesn't allow, nothing locked or kept for a rule taken off, every colonist's pieces fitting.
- **The outfit** (`WearOption.Outfit`, `ApparelPick.OptionFor`: the game's `ApparelPolicy.filter.Allows(thing)`): never
  suggested to wear past it. One piece a colonist, said as such ("Outfit Worker doesn't allow it: parka"), where it would
  fill a need nothing allowed fills as well (warmth still lacking, or more of it than the allowed pieces it would take the
  place of) or is a big upgrade (twice the threshold) with nothing allowed in its place. **Allow** sets the kind allowed
  in that outfit (`filter.SetAllow(def, true)`; the tip says how many colonists here wear it); when the outfit's quality or
  hit point limits or its dead man's filter stop it, **Outfit** opens the game's outfit window on it instead.
- **Title, role and faith** (`ApparelPick.RulesOf`): their title's and role's requirements by the game's own
  (`Pawn_ApparelTracker.AllRequirements`, `ApparelUtility.IsRequirementActive`, `ApparelRequirement.ApparelMeetsRequirement`
  with no unmatched allowance, `IsMet`), their faith's desired apparel (`Precept_Apparel.apparelDef` for their gender), their
  title's least apparel quality (`requiredMinimumApparelQuality`, a piece below it can't be suggested). A worn piece that
  meets one is kept for it (`WearPiece.Rule`): replaced only by another that meets it too. A piece that meets one not met
  now counts (above) and may fill an empty slot on that alone.
- **Keepsakes**: Rimfolk's lucky-item quirk on a piece of apparel (its mood comes with any piece of its kind) and an
  heirloom worn, read as the weapons read them; a suggestion that would take one off says so as a cost (the moods with and
  without), never a block; a colonist never asks for one that would.
- **In the game** (`Apparel/ApparelPick.cs`): a home map's colonists (slaves and children too; not babies or quest guests),
  what they wear and carry, what lies in storage (a stockpile or shelf, not forbidden or burning; an outfit stand's): the
  8 best kinds of each role by their rating, and the 8 warmest and coolest when someone lacks warmth or cooling, as many of
  each as there are colonists. Each colonist with each piece (another's worn armour too, for trades), their own rating
  kept an hour (`ApparelLive.ForColonist`) and worked out ahead a tenth of the colony every 250 ticks
  (`ApparelPickBook`, `Sched.RareApparelPicks` 43, `Pass.RareApparelPicks`); the rating as another role kept an hour. The
  choice kept per map, made again hourly, half a second after an order or "not now", or two seconds after what they wear or
  carry, their outfit or how many pieces there are changes (looked at once a second). A piece a colonist can't reach is
  taken out for them and the choice made again. How much each fights: the weapons' `FightWeight` from skills, time drafted
  and fights. Their work: the work they do first at a skill of 6 or more. The raids: the weapons' record
  (`WeaponPickBook.Seen`, new: its own raids and the game's raid letters, as the weapons read them).
- **The orders**, real jobs walked out on the map: the game's own `Wear` (from an outfit stand with the stand as its
  source), so they walk over, put it on and drop what it takes the place of, as the game's Wear does; a piece in their
  own pack set down at their feet and worn there; another's spare (`Rimfolk_TakeSpareApparel`,
  `Apparel/ApparelSwapJob.cs`: walk over, it is handed over into their pack, then put on in the piece's own equip time);
  a trade (`Rimfolk_SwapApparel`: walk over, each puts on what the other wore, whatever else either can't wear with it
  dropped). An order is the player's, so the game's optimizer keeps it on as it keeps a piece the player ordered worn.
  A button is greyed with why (no path, burning, reserved, down, the other busy). "On the way" while the job runs.
- **Where it shows** (`Apparel/ApparelPickUi.cs`, `ApparelNiceTab.cs`): the game's gear tab, "Suggested clothes" under the
  suggested weapons (its own postfix on `TryDrawComfyTemperatureRange`, at low priority); Nice Inventory Tab, by name from
  its decompile: a row of Rimfolk's own in its apparel box (`apparel_legacy_groupbox`, under the last piece worn, above
  its empty slots); its grid layout's apparel box is a grid whose code casts every cell to `ApparelGridSlot`, so there
  the row goes into the equipment box (`equipment_alt_groupbox`), under the suggested weapons' row (`WeaponNiceTab.IsSpacer`).
  The row is the weapons' (frame, tag "Suggested", "Needed", "Asked for" or "Outfit", picture, a short head without the
  colonist's name: "Warmth: parka (+40 °C)", "No helmet: flak helmet", "In place of tattered T-shirt: button-down shirt",
  badge, gain, why, a warning line for costs, **Wear**, **Take from**, **Trade with**, **Allow** or **Outfit**, **Not
  now**). The quiet line, honest about what they lack: "No warmer clothes in storage for Bautista" (warmth, cooling, body
  armour, helmet, a worn piece), else "No better clothes in storage for ...", under the rows too when a gap is left; its
  tooltip what was compared, how short they are and how cold it gets, forbidden pieces not looked at; a click the
  Defenses page. Rimfolk's apparel card: **Who should wear this** (a piece in hand; its outfit aside, the need it fills
  first). The Defenses page: **Clothes and armour for each colonist**, after the weapons: each colonist's gaps as chips
  (degrees short for the cold or heat, no body armour, no helmet, worn out, or dressed for the weather), their
  suggestions with the gain, why and a button, "Not now" or "Show again"; what the choice weighs under the heading;
  **Wear all suggested (n)** gives the orders only (never an outfit's: allow it from its row).
- **Colonists who ask** (`Apparel/ApparelAsks.cs`, "Colonists ask for better clothes", pool `Rimfolk_Pool_ApparelAsk`, 49
  lines in every tone and age, one sentence each): at their slice's hourly look, in their free time at home and safe
  (`WeaponAsks.FreeAndSafe`), a suggestion of theirs that fills a gap or gains 1.6 (`AskThreshold`), from storage, their
  pack or what their outfit doesn't allow (never a trade or another's spare, never one that takes off their own keepsake);
  at most once in six days each, once a day in the colony, the same piece not for fifteen days, not while set aside; a 10%
  chance each look, 20% for warmth while it is colder outside than they can bear. The line by its reason (warmth, cooling,
  armour, helmet, worn, dead, faith, title, role, work, mechanoids, crowds, better), "freezing" only on a cold day:
  "It's freezing; that parka in the stockpile would do me good." A quiet row in This week (How people are,
  `apparel-asks`, counted nowhere) for three days while it stands, its button the order itself.
- **Not now**: per colonist, ten days (`ApparelPickBook.notNow`), the weapons' own way.
- **Kept with the game** (`ApparelPickBook`, a GameComponent; an older save gets an empty one): "not now" and each
  colonist's last ask; modelled in `Tools/save_estimate.py`. The raids are the weapons' record.
- **Settings** (How you're told, Apparel; each on, both under "Apparel ratings" and the deeper hooks): `apparelSuggestions`
  "Apparel suggestions", `apparelAsks` "Colonists ask for better clothes". No "colonists put on missing warm clothes
  themselves": the game's own apparel optimizer already puts on what an outfit allows into an empty slot, warmth first
  when it is cold, so a Rimfolk job of its own would only race it.
- **Text:** `Languages/English/Keyed/Rimfolk_Apparel.xml` (the words the weapon suggestions share are their keys); the
  Almanac's "judging armour and clothes" (Defending, "Better clothes for each colonist", keywords unchanged).

## Algorithms, not AI

**All logic is plain rules and weights.** It's deterministic, needs no API key, works
offline, costs nothing, is fast, and can be balanced. Every wish and signal is a small
rule: "if this condition is true, propose X, fulfilled when Y."

The mod has no AI or LLM component and doesn't depend on any other mod. The flavour
comes from hand-written lines, six "tones" per wish (plain, warm, blunt, cheerful,
gloomy, cold) chosen by the colonist's traits and mood, plus vanilla social-log
interactions where colonists grumble about their wishes to each other.

**"Random but sensible"** comes from *weighted* random picks: every candidate wish gets
a weight (how bad the related thought is, how strong the passion, trait multipliers),
and the generator rolls among them. Same colony, different stories each playthrough.

---

## Fitting the world: tech level, materials, map

A medieval or tribal colony must never be asked for turrets, heaters or hospital beds it
can't build. Every suggestion goes through one gate (`Avail`):

- **Research**: a building is only suggested if its research is finished and it shows up in
  the build menu.
- **Power**: anything that needs electricity is skipped until Electricity is researched.
- **Purpose, not names**: buildings are found by what they do (heats, glows, holds
  patients, is a crafting bench for skill X, gives recreation of kind Y). So a medieval colony
  gets a torch lamp or a campfire, an industrial one a standing lamp or a heater, and modded
  furniture (e.g. Medieval Overhaul) counts automatically.
- **Materials**: room plans pick the wall and furniture material the colony has most of;
  wood counts as available when there are trees, stone blocks when there are chunks.
- **The map itself**: "tame an animal" only when tameable animals are roaming nearby,
  "bury your friend" only when the body is on the map, "a prosthetic" only when one can be
  made or is in stock, no winter advice on space maps.
- **Era of the colony**: the research advisor suggests projects from the colony's own tech
  level first.
- **Ambitions** are offered only if every goal is possible right now. "A ring of iron"
  (turrets) never comes up for a medieval colony, but "teeth in the mud" (traps) does.

### Things by what they are for (the player's request, 7 November 2026)

The player: "apply this def database to all that we created so far, if there is benefit". Where Rimfolk hands over,
sends or makes a thing that stands for a kind (a gift, food for the road, a carving), it asks one picker
(`Things/ThingRoles.cs`, its rules pure in `ThingRolesMath.cs`) instead of naming a base-game item. The picker judges
every item of the game and the player's mods by what the def says it is, never by a mod's name, so a mod's wine,
dish, statue or blade comes in on its own, and the base game's own item stays the fallback.

- **The roles.** A *drink* (a social drink with alcohol: its drug's chemical is alcohol, or it is liquor by its food
  type with no other chemical in it; worth 100 or less), a *soft drink* (one a teetotaler may have: tea, coffee), a
  *feast's dish* (a fine or lavish meal a recipe cooks, fresh), *provisions* (a simple meal or better that keeps 20
  days or more), *produce* (a sown crop, raw, not kept with the meals), *medicine*, a *precious* material (metal or
  stone that gives 2 or more beauty, nothing else besides: silver, gold, jade, Odyssey's obsidian), *small art* (a work
  of art made at a bench, a day's work or less, of wood, stone or metal; never a terror sculpture or one that holds
  the dead), a *carving* (small art that may be of wood), a *gift* (a precious material, or a drink worth 15 or more)
  and a *blade* (a melee weapon of metal that cuts or stabs, carried by the game's own weapon tags, never bonded).
- **Never anything the colony would find wrong.** Only ordinary goods: traded, nothing of a person (human meat or
  leather, a corpse), nothing to use rather than have (a comp that is used, targeted, bonded or hatches), nothing with
  a trade tag the game marks exotic (but for medicine: glitterworld medicine is the spacer age's) or that only a mod
  uses (A RimWorld of Magic's arcane metal, Deserters' contraband). What comes to the colony leaves out what most of
  its grown people at home would mind (their faith's drug rules, a teetotaler's, their diet), `Beliefs.AgainstThing`.
- **Every age.** A thing's age is its own tech level or the research its easiest recipe or crop needs, whichever is
  later; one with neither known goes with every age (Medieval 2's wine), but food that keeps only from industry on (a
  mod factory's canned soup). A giver's things are of its age (its means), the colony's own of the colony's; the age's
  own things come twice as often as older ones (a spacer colony's cocktails, a tribe's beer and mead), medicine three
  times. A gift goes by the giver's ways: a tribe's stone (jade), the middle ages' and the Empire's finest metal (gold,
  by its beauty), silver for the industrial and spacer ages, a fine drink now and then (more in the middle ages).
- **Only what the colony has unlocked.** Something the colony's own people make (a carving for a friend, a blade of
  star iron) is one it knows how to make: a recipe whose research is done (`ThingRoles.ColonyCanMake`).
- **Words match the map.** Where a letter or line names the thing, it names what was picked (its label), and a pick
  an answer's words show and its effect then makes is seeded by the answer (its people, its home) so both are the
  same. Where the words name the thing outright ("a skin of honey-beer", "a small sculpture", "a carved bird"), the
  thing stays.
- **The balance.** Amounts are by worth: a match's gift, the camp prospectors' find, a ransom's goods, a help letter's
  food come to as much silver as before whatever is picked (`ThingRolesMath.CountFor`).
- **Where.** A match's gift and the town's seasonal gift (`Matches.GiftDef`); the camp prospectors' finds
  (`CampLife.Prospected`, `GiveGoods("found")`); a tribe's ransom goods (`Ransoms.TribeGoods`, saved as a def name as
  before); a favour's medicine and food (`FavourCalls.Goods`, seeded by the tie); the envoy's parting gift (medicine
  or a gift); a help letter's food and medicine (`NeighbourLetters.HelpThings`); old friends' relief
  (`Workers_Remembered`); a guest's own provisions, one they will eat (`Hosting.Provision`); the wedding party's crop
  (`DilemmaEffect_GuestsBringFood`, `@Produce`); the animal doctor's medicine; the silent guest's parting carving, a
  stranger's carving and a regular's keepsake; a star-iron blade (one the words' "a" goes with); what an outsider may
  be asked to bring (their medicine, provisions and drink, seeded by their people); a funeral's or wedding's drinks
  (the mission's `drinks` goal: any drink in the stores, asked of a colony that brews or has ten); the journey
  planner's road food first (`ThingRolesMath.TravelRank`: what never rots, then what keeps); the founding kit's
  medicine (whichever the stores hold most of); an answer's made thing (`DilemmaEffect_Made`, `@Carving` among its
  candidates); a camp's goods put out (`@Produce` for the settlers, `@Medicine` for the healers' stall).
- **What stays as it was, and why.** Silver as money (payments, prices, ventures, rewards); the colony's own stores
  given or used (raw food, meals, medicine, wood: already any kind, PlayCarry); materials (wood, steel, components);
  animal feed (the journey's kibble and hay, by what each animal eats); the scenarios' starting kits (the game's own
  part names its item on the scenario page before anything is picked); the brewer's cart, the stash of beer and the
  smugglers' beer (their words say beer); the commission's and the likeness's small sculpture, the camp's carved bird
  (their words); a camp's own simple meals.
- **The catalogue.** `Tools/mod_pool.py` writes what the roles read into `docs/player-mods/items.tsv` (category, stack,
  tradeability, preferability, food type, drug kind and chemical, teetotaler, rot days, comps, stuff kinds and beauty,
  medical potency, what it is made of, size, minified, the age of its making, work, terror) and `weapons.tsv`
  (tradeability, comps, the age of its making, its tools' capacities). `ThingRolesTests` runs the same rules on the player's active
  rows: each role has several things in every age, the player's mods among them. Dev mode: "Things by role" (each
  role's things by age, and five picks of each for the colony and its neighbours).

---

## Playing nicely with any modlist (rules for every integration)
Rimfolk is played with a 200+ mod list (medieval before, industrial and spacer now), but must work just as well with
any other list, including a plain vanilla run. Every feature that touches another mod or a game system follows these
rules:

1. **Soft integrations only.** A mod-specific feature switches itself on when that mod is active and is simply
   absent otherwise: defs are matched by name at runtime (`GetNamedSilentFail`, type names, package ids), never by
   XML cross-references to another mod's defs, and mod-only content is gated (`MayRequire`, mod checks). Removing a
   mod mid-save must not leave errors or broken entries behind.
2. **Never harder or emptier without a mod.** Integrations add flavor and options; they don't carry the balance.
   With a mod missing, the base experience stays complete and fair.
3. **Only what the colony has unlocked.** Wishes, ambitions, advice, room plans, decrees and dilemmas only ask for or
   suggest what the colony can research, build, make or buy now. Nothing pushes the player into a tech line or a
   mod's late-game system (diplomatic marriages, faction wars) they haven't chosen to engage with.
4. **No per-run adjustment.** Era (medieval or industrial) and mods are detected automatically; medieval content stays
   out of an industrial run and the other way round.
5. **Harm at the game's own rate.** Until November 2026 moments between colonists never injured anyone (contests were
   friendly: arm wrestling, races, riddles). Since then harm may come where it's flavourful or interesting, at a rate
   comparable to the game's own chance of something bad happening, never gratuitous.
6. **Most mods get no integration, and that's fine.** A big modlist is mostly nice-to-haves the player may never use
   in a given run. Rimfolk only has to read them correctly (no false warnings, no impossible wishes, no colonist
   counted as gone). Deeper integration is kept for the few mods the player always runs, and even those stay soft.
7. **Harmony is the only hard dependency.** It's declared in About.xml, so the game's mod menu shows it and offers it
   when it's missing. Nothing else is required: no other mod's assembly is referenced, and with any other mod missing
   Rimfolk loads and plays without errors.

## Limits and risks

- **Heuristics are approximate.** Defense strength in particular is hard to compute
  (a killbox with 2 turrets beats 6 turrets in the open). Present it as "rough
  read" with confidence, not as truth.
- **Room-quality judgments.** We can read RimWorld's own room stats (impressiveness,
  space, beauty, cleanliness, role), which keeps us honest and in line with the game's
  own mood logic.
- **Modded content.** Avoid hard-coding specific buildings. Detect by category
  instead, e.g. "a bench whose recipes use the Crafting skill", or "a building that
  provides recreation". Modded benches and furniture then work automatically.
- **Performance.** Run checks every in-game hour (or less often), never every tick, each on a tick of the hour of its
  own (see "Ticking"). Cache results.
- **Exploits.** Rewards must not be farmable: cooldowns, no repeat wishes, rewards scale with effort.
- **Nagging.** The biggest design risk. Rate limits and "Not now" are essential, and
  the default is Gentle.
- **Overlap with vanilla alerts.** RimWorld already warns about some basics (e.g. no
  beds, low food). The Advisor should go beyond those (forecasts, trade-offs, *why*)
  rather than repeat them.

---

## Technical overview

Standard RimWorld mod: XML defs plus a C# assembly, depending on Harmony. Most of it hooks in
through vanilla extension points (game and map components, a main tab, inspector tabs, alerts,
thought and interaction workers, a designator, a choice letter). Where those can't reach, small
Harmony patches do (Source/ColonyCouncil/Patches): postfixes where possible, each applied on its
own so one failure doesn't stop the others, each logged once if skipped, all switchable at
runtime through the "deeper game hooks" setting. A patch has to earn its place: it changes how
the game behaves in a way the extension points can't.

```
About/About.xml, About/Preview.png
1.6/Assemblies/ColonyCouncil.dll
Defs/
  WishDefs/            # 23 data-driven wishes with flavour lines (add new ones in XML)
  AdvisorSignalDefs/   # 14 advisor checks with "why it matters" tips
  AmbitionDefs/        # 20 ambitions with goals and pitch lines
  RoomTemplateDefs/    # 13 room templates for the planner
  ThoughtDefs/         # wish granted, ambition achieved, spoke up for me, ...
  InteractionDefs/     # colonists talking about their wishes and the ambition
  Misc/                # the Council main tab and the meeting letter
Languages/English/Keyed/
Patches/               # one conditional addition: the strain part on global work speed
Textures/ColonyCouncil/
Source/ColonyCouncil/  # C#; builds against the Krafs.Rimworld.Ref NuGet package
Tools/DefValidator/    # offline XML checker against the real game types
Tools/ApiDiff/         # will the built DLL still run on another game version?
Tools/Tests/           # tests for the room rotation math
Tools/make_icons.py    # draws the interface icons (Textures/ColonyCouncil/Icons) and their contact sheet
Tools/perf_audit.py    # ranks the code's hot spots without the game (docs/perf-audit.md)
Tools/save_estimate.py # how each saved collection grows over five years (docs/save-size.md)
```

Core types:

- `WishDef` / `WishWorker`: a worker lists candidate wishes for a colonist (with a weight
  and a reason) and says when a wish is fulfilled.
- `Wish`: the live, saved instance (who asked, for whom, about whom, expiry, quote, co-signers).
- `CouncilGameComponent`: generates, tracks, grants and expires wishes hourly; owns the
  ambition tracker and personal touches; tells the chronicle (`AddChronicle`, into the one history).
- `AdvisorSignalDef` / `AdvisorSignalWorker` + `CouncilMapComponent`: advice per map,
  refreshed hourly, ranked by severity, urgency and confidence.
- `AmbitionDef` + goal classes + `AmbitionTracker`: council meetings and the active ambition.
- `RoomTemplateDef`, `TemplatePlanner`, `Designator_PlanRoom`: room plans with a ghost preview,
  rotation, material choice and a spot finder.
- `Avail`: the tech, research, material and purpose checks described above.
- `MainTabWindow_Council`, `MainTabWindow_World`, `MainTabWindow_Defenses`, `MainTabWindow_Planning`: the four
  windows (see "Rimfolk's windows").

Things the game exposes that this relies on (all available to mods):

| Need | Game data |
|---|---|
| Pawn's bad thoughts | Mood thought list per pawn |
| Bedroom and room quality | Owned bed and room, room role, room stats (impressiveness, space, beauty) |
| Traits, passions, skills | Trait set, skill records with passion level |
| Work assignments | Work priorities per work type |
| Partners | Direct relations (lover, spouse, fiancé) |
| Raid strength | Storyteller threat points, colony wealth |
| Food | Total human-edible nutrition on the map |
| Seasons | Average temperature per twelfth for the map's tile, growing-season check |
| Power | Power net gain rate and stored energy |
| Building | Placing standard blueprints (so pawns build them normally) |
| Rewards | Mood memories, inspirations |

### Homes: what a colony is

A colony is a player home map, known by its settlement's world object id (`map.Parent.ID`, which outlives the map's
own id). `Lean/Homes.cs` is the one place that says which; its rules are pure (`Lean/HomesMath.cs`) and tested.

- `Homes.All`: the player's homes in the order they were founded, those on the ground before those in orbit.
- `Homes.Seat`: the colony the council sits at. The first home founded, unless a seat is stored (a saved id, set by
  "Make this the seat" on a colony's card: below, "A fresh start") and is still a home. It doesn't move as people do.
- `Homes.Of(pawn)`: the colony someone belongs to. On a home map now (held there too, as in a casket): that one. Else
  the home where they own a bed. Else the last home they lived on (set once they've been on it a day without a break,
  kept per colonist, forgotten once they're dead, discarded or no longer the colony's). Else the seat.
- `Homes.People(map)`: the free colonists who belong to a home; a meeting's members are those of them with a say.
- `Homes.Name(map)`: the settlement's name, for texts that have to tell two colonies apart.
- `Homes.Changed`: a home founded or lost, noticed in the council's hour (the council's book of colonies listens: below).
- `Homes.LastHome(pawn)`: the last home someone lived on for a day, while it's still a home.

With one colony every answer is that colony, so it plays as before. `MapFacts.BusiestHome` and
`HappeningTracker.HomeMap()` (the seat, on the ground) keep their names but return the seat; "the colony" used to be
the home with the most colonists on it, which moved as people did. New code asks `Homes`: the seat for what the colony
as a whole has, a loop over `Homes.All` for what each home has, and `Homes.Busiest` only for what follows people about
(nothing asks it since social events are worked out at each home, step 7b). Rimfolk's own event timer runs per home (the seat carries on an older
save's single timer), a memo keeps its colony so its follow-up (a guest, goods brought back, an order collected) comes
where it was set going, talks with visitors start on every home, and a raid is written up by those at the home raided.

### Many homes

Each colony has a council of its own (stage 0, step 7a): `ColonyState`, one per colony, known by its key
(`Homes.KeyOf`), kept in the council component's `colonies` and saved with it (the council already runs and saves
everything it holds, so the trackers stay what they were and only move one level down). Its rules are pure
(`Lean/ColonyStateMath.cs`) and tested (`Tools/Tests/ColonyStateTests.cs`). `ColonyState.For(map)` gives a home's (the
seat's for a map that isn't a home), made when a home first needs one; `ColonyState.Of(pawn)` someone's
(`Homes.Of`); `ColonyState.Ticking()` the councils that run this hour, each home's in the order they were founded.

**Per colony now.**
- *Offices and elections* (`OfficeTracker`): one set of seats per colony. Only its own people at home vote and stand;
  the election is held at its own home, by its own year; its peacemaker cools rivalries between its own people; a
  seat's edge and the colony-wide edges reach only its people. An officer who has gone to live at another colony (there
  now, and a day there) steps down; away on a caravan or a short visit they keep the seat. `OfficeTracker.HeldBy(pawn)`
  finds anyone's office, their own colony's first. The elders sit with their own colony's young; days as physician
  and marshal count in every colony.
- *Ambition and meeting* (`AmbitionTracker`): one ambition and one meeting per colony, each at its own home
  (`MeetingMap`); the meeting's gathering, its waking and its letter find their colony by the map. One whose home is no
  longer ours ends quietly (clean-up asks "still our home", not "is the map still there").
- *Decrees* (`DecreeTracker`): one per colony. What makes it needed, its petitions, the threats it counts, its tithes
  and alms (from its own stores, stretched by its own quartermaster, the goodwill to the nearest friendly settlement
  measured from its home), its hediffs, curfew hours, practice, banked fires, grief fading, the backlash of a repeat and
  the daily trust are all its own people's and home's. The declaration's letter counts its own for and against. Decree
  moods, the heart's strain and relief, a quarantine's contagion, a clean sweep's work order and the petitions' setback
  read the decrees of the person's own colony. The one faith a decree names is still one for the game.
- *Dilemmas and traditions* (`DilemmaTracker`): each colony keeps its own rhythm, cooldowns (the pool's colony key)
  and traditions, and casts its questions at its own home; a raid's aftermath is asked at the colony raided. A question
  waiting for its answer holds back only its own colony (one about no colony, or a home no longer ours, holds back all).
  The answer goes to the council of the colony it's about. Secrets, a coming of age, kin in the cells and a partner from
  outside ask the colony concerned.
- *Wishes and trust*: the wishes stay one list, each counted under the colony of the one who asked. Each colony rolls
  for its own wishes, from its own people, under its own decrees and its own cap on open wishes (the event wishes, a
  dream's and an envious one's too); a petition is joined only within a colony; the speaker raises trust in their own
  colony; "never the colony's last few people" counts each colony's own; `ColonyTrust(map)` and the steward's hold on
  standards are per colony. Trust itself stays per person.

**Per colony too (stage 0, step 7b).** The other books kept per colony follow the council's rules through one helper,
`ColonyBook` (in `ColonyState.cs`: a home's entry made when first needed, the seat's for a map that isn't a home, an old
save's single entry placed at the seat, a lost home's kept thirty days and carried by its people when no home is left),
over any `IColonyEntry`.
- *Happenings*: a later event picks up only its own colony's memos (`Memos(kind, days, map)`, `HomesMath.MemoAt`; an
  old memo, or one of a home no longer ours, is the seat's): a rematch, a beast's young, pilgrims' thanks, a regular
  buyer, a quarrel remembered, a guest expected, an orphaned young, a commission and its patron. Those that follow a
  person on the map (a deserter, a lost child's finder, lovers, kin, a bad fortune) were per home already. An
  unanswered event letter holds back only its own colony (`WaitingAt(map)`, `HomesMath.HoldsBack`; one about no colony,
  or a home no longer ours, holds back all).
- *Calendar*: one per colony (`Calendar/ColonyCalendar.cs`, kept in the calendars' book, `CalendarTracker`, the same
  saved component). Each settlement has its own founding day (the game's start for a colony settled in the game's
  first two days, else the day its settlement was made: `CalendarMath.FoundedTick`), its own days, date (`seenDay`,
  `seenYear`), rest day, talk and traditions, and keeps them at its own home; a day's letter keeps its colony and holds
  back only that colony's days. A victory is filed at the battle's colony, a death at the dead's, a wedding, a foal, a
  companion and a camp's gift at their own; harvest, snow, homecomings, hunts, trades, rescues, the first child and
  one of the first members (joined in its own first year: `CalendarMath.FirstMember`) are read from each colony's own
  people and land. The seat's calendar keeps what is the colony's as a whole: the nemeses and the world's events. The
  founding event keeps only the founding day of the colony settled with the game; a later colony keeps its own. The
  Calendar page shows the colony in view (with the colony header); the region window's Here and away, This week
  and the HUD list each colony's coming days, named.
- *Officers at work*: Interplay's officers are each colony's (`Interplay.Officer(def, map)`, `OfficerOf`, `Holds`,
  `Officers`): the keeper of days, the peacemaker, the steward and the chaplain of the colony where it happens; each
  colony's physician, herdmaster (`AnimalFacts.HerdmasterAt`, `IsHerdmaster`), chaplain, warden and marshal keep their
  own days. The chaplain's faith factor, a steward's thrift, the speaker who writes the neighbour letters and leads a
  talk, a scenario's first council, an office a question asks for, and the annals' list of seats (each colony's,
  named) read the colony concerned. A quarantine shuts only its own gates (`DecreeWork.VisitorFactor(map)`: with one
  colony it stays in the storyteller's base chance, with more it is in the event's chance at its target).
- *Questions asked of the colony concerned*: the harvest home, supper and name-the-year traditions an event reads, a
  camp's trouble, the resident beast, a guest's invitation and their kin, a shared name and a guardian (each colony's
  council looks among its own), asking again after someone was kept from moving on.
- *Camps*: one `CampHome` per colony (in `CampTracker.homes`): its visiting camp, its neighbours settled for good, its
  war party, and its own clock (the day's try, the gap since its last camp, the diary: `CampStoryMath.RepickTry`,
  `InGap`, `PutOff`). Camps are rolled at each home on the ground; allies answer a threat at any home;
  `CampTracker.VisitingAt(map)`, `HoldingAt`, `WarBandAt` are what everything else asks.
- *Encounters, the herd and the beast*: strangers are met at each home on its own (`EncounterHome`: the day's count,
  the last, each kind's cooldown; their questions asked of that colony); the herd's year and the beast that stays are
  one per colony (`comp.HerdOf(map)`, `BeastOf(map)`).
- *The social web*: a fight per home (`Social/Battle.cs`, `SocialWeb.BattleAt(map)`, `BattleOn`, `AnyBattle`): two
  fights at two homes are two fights, and a victory is felt at the home that fought it. Social events are worked out
  and held at each home. Groups form within one home (`GroupMath.Apart`: people of two colonies hold to each other not
  at all, so they never form, join or merge one group, and someone who moved away drifts out of their old one).
- *The year's letter*: with more than one colony, a part for each colony under its name (its herd, its beast, its
  neighbours), then the world once. The annals count big threats at each home (two raids at once are two) and compare
  the whole colony's wealth; the Overview's wealth tile names each colony's.
- *Names*: a colony key on each name (`EpithetMath.Key`; the name alone with one colony, as always): the Healer is the
  best healer of that colony, and taking a name over makes a rival only within one colony. A name from one colony's
  days belongs to its holder's colony. The game's founders and firstborn are the colony settled with the game, else the
  seat's (`EpithetMath.FirstColony`); a colony settled later has its own (those who were its people in its first two
  days, the first child on its own calendar).
- *The advisor and automations*: with more than one colony "Not this" is set at the home it's said at
  (`SuggestMath.HomeKey`, the list to bring it back names the settlement), a step done waits for its check only at its
  home (`SuggestMath.SameHome`), and an automation's cooldowns, materials budget and daily caps are each home's own
  (research stays one). What was set aside with one colony stays set aside everywhere. The game-wide advice (a mission
  near its deadline, a plague or famine, a colony split between faiths) shows at each home on the ground.
- *Journeys*: one plan per home at most (`JourneyBook.PlanAt(map)`, `PlanOf(pawn)`), each setting off from its own home.
- *News*: what was told with no map but is about a home goes through `Tell` with it, so it names the settlement.

**Still one for the game**: the chronicle and the annals (one book, each colony named in it, the Chronicle page filtered
by the colony in view since release 4), the wishes' list, trust, the heart's episodes, the remembered camps that may come
back, the world's news. The colony's character was one until stage 3's release 4 made it each colony's own (below, "Many
colonies in play"). The one faith
a decree names stays one for the game: the game keeps one faith per people (`Faction.OfPlayer.ideos`), not per map, so
two colonies naming two faiths would pull the same people two ways. `comp.offices`, `decrees`, `ambitions` and
`dilemmas` still read the seat's council where the colony as a whole is meant.

**An old save** puts everything it had under its one colony: its offices, election, decrees, ambition, meeting,
dilemmas and traditions become the seat's council, untouched (`ColonyState.FromOldSave`, placed when the seat first
asks). An election letter from before has no map and reads the seat's council. Its calendar, camps and their clock, a
fight going on, encounters, herd, beast and journey plan are read from where they always were into the seat's entry
(each book reads the old fields into an entry with no home, which the seat takes); its names stay under the name alone
and count for the colony of the one who holds them; its memos, letters and suggestions with no colony are the seat's
(or everywhere, for "Not this").

**A home lost** (abandoned, taken, handed over; `Homes.Changed`): a meeting, an election and an ambition there end
quietly; the council is kept thirty days (`ColonyStateMath.KeepLostDays`) in case the home comes back, then let go.
With no home left, its people carry it, and the next home founded (the seat) takes it; a new seat that is the only home
and has no council yet takes the one of the home just left. So a colony that moves keeps its council, whether it gives
up the old home first, lands a gravship, or settles and gives up the old home within the hour. A colony founded beside
the first has a council of its own, and people who move to a colony that has one join it.

**The pages** show the colony in view (`UI/ColonyView.cs`: the map on screen when it's a home, else the seat): the
Decrees page with the offices and the election, the Ambition and Dilemmas pages, the council HUD panel, the calendar's
election and traditions, the Council tab's counts. With more than one colony those pages name the colony at the top
("The council of Oakhold (the seat)") with a button to go to another colony, which changes the map in view. This
week lists every colony's petitions and meetings, each named; texts that mix colonies name the settlement through
`Tell`.

With one colony there is one council, every colony check is that colony (`ColonyState.Has` and `Of` answer it at once),
the same people are taken in the same order, and the same rolls are made in the same order: it plays as before. Step
7b keeps to the same: lists are filtered by colony, never sorted again; each per-home loop has one pass with one home;
keys (names, suggestions, automations' cooldowns) are what they always were with one colony; and where the place of a
roll moved (a quarantine's factor) it stays where it was with one colony. Tests: `Tools/Tests/ManyHomesTests.cs`.

#### A fresh start (stage 3, release 1)

A new colony founded in the same world, without giving up the one there is (docs/design/stage3-many-colonies.md,
section 1 without a scenario's parts, 3a and 3c; the player's decisions of 6 November 2026). `Source/ColonyCouncil/Colonies/`:
the rules are pure (`FoundingMath.cs`, tested in `Tools/Tests/FoundingTests.cs`); `Foundings.cs` runs it in the
council's hour, right after the homes (`Homes.Hourly`), and only while there is a founding or a question about moving
(nothing per tick, no schedule slot); the place picker and the founding window are `FoundingWindow.cs`, the newcomers'
window `NewcomersWindow.cs`, the questions `FoundingLetters.cs`, the seat `ColonySeat.cs`, the cards and the Ours lens
`ColonyCards.cs`; what it keeps rides the homes' own component (`HomesFounding.cs`).
- **The place.** "Found a new colony" on a colony's card (a home on the ground, one founding at a time) opens the
  game's world targeter (`WorldTargeter.BeginTargeting`), with Rimfolk's facts of the tile under the cursor beside it
  (`FoundingPlace.Facts`): whose land (Faction Territories, `WorldMechanics.TerritoryOwner`), the towns within 12 tiles
  and their stance, how remote (`RegionMath.Remoteness`, the region's own five words), the days by caravan from each
  home (the game's estimate), the land, and the game's checks (`TileFinder.IsValidTileForNewSettlement`, the goodwill
  a nearby town loses each season, `SettlementProximityGoodwillUtility`).
- **Who goes (decision 2A).** The founding window lists the home's people (`Homes.People`), grown-ups first; children
  follow their parents unless moved. Each grown-up's wish comes from their own ties (`FoundingMath.Pull`: their own, a
  partner, child or parent, going or staying ±3 each; at odds with most here by the fights the council counts +2;
  close friends ±1, rivals the other way; a seat on the council, a room of their own, old age -1 each; youth +1; past
  1.5 either way "wants to go" or "wants to stay", else "torn"), with the reasons. Nobody refuses. Sent or kept against
  it (`AgainstWish`), they feel uprooted for a season (`Rimfolk_Uprooted`, -4, 15 days) and, with the old colony kept,
  may ask once between the third day and the season's end to move to the colony they wanted (`FoundingAsk`, a
  `Tell.Ask`: a journey plan of one, or asked to stay at 2 trust). Close bonds split between the two colonies (a
  partner, a parent or child, a sibling, a friend of 60) feel parted for a season (`Rimfolk_Parted`, -3, the three
  closest at most). Who may go: this home's people, at home, not a lodger, not being banished, not on another journey
  (`CantSend`); the party needs a grown-up, and the old colony kept needs one left in it (`PartyCheck`).
- **How they go.** By caravan through the journey planner's own plan (`Foundings.PlanJourney`: one way, a
  `JourneyPlan.founding` id, food for the road and fifteen days more, the founding kit by the colony's age from what the
  stores hold: wood for a tribe or a medieval colony, steel, components and a little wood for industry and beyond,
  medicine for the first season; fitted to 90% of the party's room, fewer days of food first, then less of the
  materials), and the planner opens on it. Its farewell at the gate is a parting's (`Rimfolk_Pool_FoundingSays`). By the
  colony's own pods or shuttle (a launcher there), or the gravship (Odyssey's engine there): the game's own way, told
  in a letter. A caravan of theirs stopped at the place or within two tiles is asked once "Settle here?"
  (`ChoiceLetter_Founding`), which runs the game's own `SettleInEmptyTileUtility.Settle` with its proximity warning;
  the game's Settle button works the same. Any home made since the founding set out at the place (anywhere, for the
  gravship's landing) is the new colony. Nobody from the colony: the newcomers alone, the settlement made with
  `SettleUtility.AddNewHome` and its map with `GetOrGenerateMapUtility.GetOrGenerateMap` in the game's long events.
- **Newcomers (decisions 3A and 4A).** Made with `Dialog_Newcomers`, built as the game's `Dialog_ChooseNewWanderers`:
  a fresh `GameInitData`, one to six people with `StartingPawnUtility` (the portrait area and character card with its
  randomize, Biotech's options, health, relations, possessions, the skills summary), the player's people's kind; the
  start data cleared however the window closes. At once with nobody going, else asked for once the colony stands (a
  letter; unanswered, let go after 10 days). They walk in from the edge with their possessions, as the game's own new
  wanderers do. Free with the old colony abandoned in the same act; with it kept, at most once a year
  (`Homes.newcomersPaidAt`), their passage paid from the old colony's stores, about their kit's worth, at least 150
  each, up to half in food (`FoundingMath.Passage`, `Pay`), named at the window's foot before Confirm. A scenario's
  start parts come in release 3, through the window's request.
- **The colony stands** (`Foundings.Founded`): the record of every colony on the world ledger (`LedgerColony`, below),
  a milestone `colony:founded` (the founders "did", the mother colony "about"), a letter naming the founders, the party's
  age form (a band to make a new hearth, settlers with a charter and carts, a settlement company, a colony mission) and
  what becomes of the old colony, the seat moved if asked, the moods above, and on the old colony's calendar (kept) the
  parting day (`CalendarKind.Parting`, a remembrance that may become a tradition). Its own council, calendar from its
  founding day, founders and firstborn come from 7a and 7b's rules. Its first evening (17 to 21h, two hours after it
  stands at least) is a fire (`PlayKind.Bonfire`, laid from the wood they brought if there's none): the founders
  invited, a seat holder among them or the eldest organising, their words from `Rimfolk_Pool_FirstNight`, and
  `Rimfolk_FirstNight` (+4, 4 days) held until it is over; with answers not played out, the speaker's line and the mood.
- **The old colony.** Kept, a second home under the game's limit. Or abandoned: once the new colony stands and none of
  the party is still on the old map (a straggler holds it back, and the colony is told once), the game's own
  `MapParent.Abandon` at the next frame, then `GameEnder.CheckOrUpdateGameOver`; anyone left there is lost to the
  colony as the game rules, and the window named them. Its council goes with its people to the new home
  (`FoundingMath.CarryCouncil`, 7a's rule as a gravship landing carries it), its record ends "abandoned" with the
  game's ruin, the milestone `colony:abandoned`, and its founding day stays on the new calendar as a remembrance. Any
  home on the record that is lost another way ends there too (`Foundings.HomesLost`: abandoned when the game's ruin
  stands at its place, else lost).
- **The game's colony limit (decision 5B).** `Prefs.MaxNumberOfPlayerSettlements` is the game's preference, shared by
  every save: as the founding starts, Rimfolk raises it by one when the new colony would pass it, never past the game's
  five (`FoundingMath.LimitFor`, against the homes the game counts), and the founding window says so plainly, with
  where to lower it again. With the old colony abandoned, or the founding called off, it is set back by one while it
  is still what Rimfolk set and the homes left fit (`LimitBack`).
- **The record of every colony** (`World/Ledger/LedgerColonies.cs`): `LedgerColony` per colony (its key, name, tile,
  founding day, the colony it came from, how and when it ended, the ruin it left), 24 at most (the oldest ended ones
  fold into the history), written only once a second colony is founded.
- **The seat (decision 1A).** "Make this the seat" on a colony's card, a home on the ground of several, at most once a
  season (`FoundingMath.SeatWhyNot`, `Homes.seatMovedAt`), or ticked in the founding window for the new colony. What
  reads `Homes.Seat` moves with it: the events and letters about no home of their own (`HappeningTracker.HomeMap`), the
  seat's council (`comp.offices` and the others, the speaker who signs to the world), the seat's calendar's world days
  and nemeses from then on, the notables and world events anchored at the seat (release 4 gives every home its own),
  the region map's default. Each colony's own council, calendar and names stay. The old seat's people lose 3 trust
  (not a mood); the milestone `colony:seat`; the seat's word by age (`AgeFeature.Seat`: the elders' fire, the
  council's hall, the town hall, the administration).
- **Seeing every colony (3c).** The region map's Ours lens lists every home however far (beyond the map's reach too),
  each row its grown-ups and children, speaker, mood and strain, its card's lines on hover (founded when and from
  where, the seat or not, wealth, its next day by name and date, a threat now); a founding on its way; and the colonies
  of the past (group 3), founded and ended how. A colony's card: go there, make this the seat, found a new colony, and
  with a founding under way plan the party's journey, choose the newcomers or call it off; a colony of the past has a
  card from its record. With more than one colony every view's header carries a chip naming the colony in view, a
  click from another (`ColonyView.Chip`, drawn by `UiKit.ViewHeader`); the council pages' own line it replaces.
- **Settings.** "Many colonies" on the What's on page: Fresh starts, and Newcomers under it. Off, nothing new is
  offered; a founding under way goes on.
- **Seams.** Release 2's hand-over is the founding window's third choice for the old colony and a card act beside
  these (marked `HandOver`); release 3's scenario parts shape the newcomers' request; release 4 widens the seat-anchored
  notables and world events to every home. With one colony nothing runs: no founding, no question, nothing saved (each
  new list is written only when it holds something), and the Ours lens's home row reads the same people as before in
  more words.

#### A scenario's start (stage 3, release 3)

Any loaded scenario can shape a new colony alone (docs/design/stage3-many-colonies.md, section 1, "A scenario's start";
the player's decision 3A of 6 November 2026). Pure rules in `Colonies/ScenarioStartMath.cs` (`Tools/Tests/ScenarioStartTests.cs`,
prefix "scenario start: "); the game's side in `Colonies/ScenarioStarts.cs` (reading a scenario, making its people and
kit, their arrival, Rimfolk's parts at the new colony), `ScenarioStartWindow.cs` (the list), `ScenarioStartPatches.cs`
(the pawn hooks), with seams in `NewcomersWindow.cs`, `FoundingWindow.cs`, `Foundings.cs` and `HomesFounding.cs`.
- **The choice.** With newcomers called, the founding window asks their start: new people as a new game's group (as
  before), or a scenario's start, chosen in `Dialog_ScenarioStart` from every scenario def loaded (the game's, its DLCs',
  Rimfolk's seventeen, other mods'), this game's own when it is none of those, and the player's own and the workshop's
  the game already holds (`ScenarioStarts.Loaded`; nothing read from the disk mid-game). For each: what comes for the
  new colony alone, what isn't carried, what never comes, and that a whole new scenario on its own page is what a new
  game is for. The founding plan keeps it by a key (`FoundingPlan.scenario`, `ScenarioStartMath.Key`: "def:", "game",
  "file:", "workshop:"); not loaded any more when the newcomers are chosen, they come as a new game's group.
- **What each part does** (`ScenarioStartMath.Carry`, by the part's class as the game names it). Carried: the people
  (the four `ScenPart_ConfigPage_ConfigureStartingPawns*` parts), what shapes starting people (forced trait and hediff,
  naked, a need's level, the age filter, no possessions), the kit (defined things, mechs, what it scatters near the start
  or anywhere), the animals, the arrival, and Rimfolk's own thirteen. Not carried, listed by what they change: the
  scenario's own people when it isn't the colony's kind, starting research, rules for every map, its own kind of map,
  world conditions, incidents switched off, the whole game's events (quests and incidents made at the start, the
  monolith, the pursuing mechanoids), the opening words. Another mod's part, even one built on the game's, is listed as
  not carried; with the deeper game hooks off, so are the parts that shape people through them. Never: Bad Blood's
  watches (`ScenPart_CouncilFamilies`), a feud that began aboard their ship.
- **The people.** `Dialog_Newcomers` reads the people part's fields into its own start data (`ScenarioStarts.InitData`:
